1.pericope_label: The Lord reigneth: clouds and darkness round about him, and the hills melting like wax

schools.summary: Augustine refers the restored land of the title to the resurrection of the flesh, after which all that the psalm sings was done.

Calvin argues that the psalm cannot describe the kingdom under the Law and must predict the kingdom of the gospel, and takes the clouds plainly as a symbol meant to impress reverence, refusing the refined reading that makes them a check on curiosity; Gill reports a Jewish reading of the melting hills as the kings of the wicked.

Henry allows that the dispensations are unaccountable while holding that a golden thread of justice runs through the whole web of the administration, and applies the isles to his own country; Spurgeon notes how many victories of the faith have been won on actual islands and observes that a land isolated by the sea is spared desolation.

Clarke leaves the authorship open after reviewing the versions, gives in full the refined reading of the clouds that Calvin rejects, builds the opening proposition on three divine names, and points out that the passage animates the throne and the elements alike; Wesley keeps the isles to the Gentile nations.

Ellicott dates the psalm from its westward geography and traces the clouds to the theophany on the mountain, finding in them not fear but a sense of safety; Keil and Delitzsch dismiss the ascription to David, call the psalm mosaic-work out of older psalms and prophets, and list its echoes verse by verse.

debates: When and by whom was the psalm written? Keil and Delitzsch call the ascription to David worthless and the psalm post-exilic mosaic-work made out of earlier psalms and prophets, nothing but echoes of the older literature; Ellicott reaches the same date from the wide westward glance at the isles, characteristic of post-exile writing; Clarke reviews the versions and the manuscripts and leaves the author uncertain, noting that the psalm is much in the spirit of David finest compositions while many learned men refer it to the restoration; Calvin and Augustine refer the whole to the kingdom of Christ.

What do the clouds and darkness signify? Calvin takes them plainly, as a symbol meant to impress reverence, and expressly rejects as a refinement the reading that makes them a check on presumptuous curiosity, though he grants that reading a useful lesson; Clarke gives precisely that reading in full, since God is infinite and there must be an impenetrable obscurity round about him; Ellicott traces the imagery to the mountain and holds that its immediate effect on the Hebrew mind was not fear but a sublime sense of safety in the established right of God; Henry keeps the unaccountable dispensations and the golden thread of justice together.
outliers: Clarke builds the opening proposition on three divine names, one for infinite being and universal government, one for the Director and Judge who shows men good and evil, and one for the God who enters into a gracious covenant to help our infirmity.

Spurgeon observes that some of the greatest victories of the faith have been won upon actual islands, instancing Polynesia and the kingdom of Madagascar, and remarks that many a land owes its peace to the sea, since if it had not been isolated it would have been desolated.
themes: a reign announced as the theme
justice as the foundation of the throne

6.pericope_label: The heavens declare his righteousness: the confusion of idolaters and the gladness of Zion

schools.summary: Spurgeon holds the shame of idolaters certain and summons the heathen deities by name to lay down their emblems at the cross; Henry likens the kingdom to the pillar of cloud and fire, dark on one side and bright on the other, and observes that though all the earth was bidden rejoice, only Zion does.
Gill leaves the seventh verse between a prayer and a prophecy, and offers three senses for the heavens that declare, the tokens of wrath, the inhabitants of heaven, and the ministers of the gospel.

Clarke identifies the one to be worshipped as Jesus on the apostle authority and the gods as his angels, notices a wordplay describing idolaters as moving like madmen, and makes the heavens intelligent beings whose order proclaims their maker; Wesley keeps the verse as a wish and the daughters of Judah as the people to whom the King came.

Ellicott denies that the word means angels and traces the quotation in the epistle to the law rather than to this psalm, doubts that the verbs are imperatives, and corrects the number of the peoples who at length see what Israel had seen through the cloud; Keil and Delitzsch agree on the source of the quotation and hold the verb a perfect of what actually takes place.

debates: Whom does the seventh verse summon, and where does the epistle take its quotation from? Clarke answers that the one worshipped is Jesus on the apostle authority and that the gods are his angels, as the old Greek renders and the apostle quotes; Ellicott denies both, holding that the word is not angels but the very agencies the heathen worshipped as deities, and that the quotation in the epistle comes from the Greek of a passage in the law; Keil and Delitzsch agree with Ellicott on both points.

Do the verbs of the seventh verse command or report? Keil and Delitzsch hold the verb no imperative at all, since as a command the clause would be abrupt and inconsequential, but the perfect of what actually takes place; Ellicott doubts the imperative more cautiously and thinks a fact is stated; Gill leaves it between a prayer and a prophecy; Wesley keeps the wish and Spurgeon the certainty.
outliers: Clarke notices a play on the letters by which those who boast of idols are described as moving like madmen, and refers it to the violent gestures practised in idolatrous rites.
Spurgeon summons the heathen deities by name to do homage, bidding one lay down his hammer at the foot of the cross and another remove his blood-stained car out of the road.
themes: a summons that may be a statement
one event dark to some and bright to others
joy confined to those who welcome the reign

10.pericope_label: Ye that love the Lord, hate evil: light sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright

schools.summary: Spurgeon holds that we cannot love God without hating what he hates and must be in arms against evil, and turns the sown light into a morning advancing with rosy steps.

Gill reports the ancient versions which render that light is risen rather than sown, cites an old poet for light as a figure of gladness, and extends the hatred of evil from sin to the conduct of evil men.

Clarke makes the light and the gladness seeds requiring cultivation, holds that God will not give more grace until we improve what we have, calls all other joy the mirth of fools, and leaves the reader free to take the whole psalm of Christ and the last judgment; Wesley reduces the sowing to a laying up in store.

Ellicott defends the psalmist against the charge of compiling and calls him at the close a true poet, prefers to point the opening words as a statement rather than a command, and cites a heathen dialogue on the common root of love and hate; Keil and Delitzsch allow this strophe alone to be original while suspecting it a later addition, and correct the ancient versions on the sowing of light.

debates: Is the psalm a compilation or a poem? Keil and Delitzsch, having called the earlier verses nothing but echoes of the older literature, allow only this closing strophe to be original and suspect even that of being a later addition; Ellicott answers that notwithstanding the points of similarity with earlier psalms the writer shows himself at the close more than a compiler, a true poet.

Is the light sown or risen? Keil and Delitzsch hold that the ancient versions misapprehended the figure in reading a rising where the text has a sowing, and explain the sowing as a strewing along the man way so that he advances step by step in the light; Gill reports those same versions and the paraphrase without objection; Clarke keeps the sowing and makes light and gladness seeds that must be cultivated; Wesley reduces it to a laying up in store.
outliers: Ellicott supports the duty of hating evil from a heathen dialogue in which Philosophy says that love and hate spring from the same source, and the writer answers that his own business is to hate the bad and to love and commend the good, and that he sticks to it.
Clarke ends by noting that the whole psalm has been understood by several of the ancient fathers of Christ and the last judgment, and leaves the reader free to take it in either sense.
themes: love of God measured by hatred of evil
souls preserved though bodies are not
light strewn along a way rather than risen
joy that is not the mirth of fools
